analysis.one_liner: Guarantees health benefits to retired coal miners whose employers went out of business, paid by premiums on coal producers.
analysis.headline: The bill creating guaranteed health care for retired coal miners left behind by closed companies was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in November 1991 and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a government corporation to pay medical and death benefits to "orphan miners" — retired coal miners and their widows whose health coverage collapsed when their employers went out of business or pulled out of union plans. To pay for it, every coal producer would owe 75 cents per hour worked in coal production, coal importers would owe an equivalent per-ton fee, and companies that signed coal wage agreements would owe annual premiums for the retirees attributed to them. The bill also merged the aging union benefit plans into a new United Mine Workers of America 1991 Benefit Fund and directed excess pension assets to shore up the retiree plans. It died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired coal miners and their spouses, widows, and dependents who were eligible for retiree health care from union-negotiated plans but were no longer receiving it because their employer left the industry or shut down — the "orphan miners" the bill names. The bill guarantees them medical benefits substantially equal to what their old plans provided, plus death benefits, funded industry-wide instead of by whichever companies happened to remain. It also stabilizes the remaining contributing employers and the union benefit funds by spreading legacy retiree costs across all producers and importers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired coal miners and their widows

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Coal Industry Retiree Health Benefit Corporation to provide medical and death benefits to orphan miners — retired miners whose employer plans failed — and to their spouses, surviving spouses, and dependents.

Funds the benefits through an hourly premium of 75 cents on every hour worked in coal production, an equivalent per-ton premium on imported coal, and annual per-beneficiary premiums from signatory employers, so retiree health care no longer depends on any one company staying in business.

Merges the financially troubled closed retiree plans into a new United Mine Workers of America 1991 Benefit Fund and directs excess pension assets first to the new Corporation and the Fund, to eliminate plan deficits.

Requires the last signatory operator to keep providing retiree health benefits to anyone receiving them as of February 1, 1993, for as long as that operator remains in business, closing an escape hatch for companies considering leaving the plans.

analysis.who_pays: Coal producers pay 75 cents per hour worked in coal production; importers pay an equivalent 15-cents-per-ton premium; and companies that signed the coal wage agreements pay annual per-beneficiary premiums for the retirees attributed to them, with their corporate parents jointly and severally liable. Because premiums are tax-deductible, part of the cost is absorbed by the Treasury. Some of the premium cost would likely be passed through to coal prices and, ultimately, electricity customers. Retirees also bear cost-containment tradeoffs: the bill mandates managed care with drug formularies, Medicare-level physician payment caps, and utilization review.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal producers, importers, and signatory operators

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new mandatory payments on all coal producers and importers, whether or not they employ union labor or owe anything to the failing plans, and those costs can be passed on in coal and electricity prices.

Beneficiaries face mandatory managed care: drug formularies, physician payments capped at Medicare allowable charges, and utilization review procedures — cost containment the bill builds in to keep the program self-sufficient.
Benefit levels are capped at what the old plans provided, not increased, and benefits are reduced by any Medicare or other government coverage the retiree already receives.

Excess pension assets are redirected to retiree health plans with special tax treatment and immunity from penalties, and the Corporation's receipts and disbursements are exempt from the federal budget — design choices that reduced oversight and revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For retired miners and widows who had lost or were losing health coverage they earned over decades of mine work, the benefit is substantial and concrete: a funded, guaranteed benefit program. The costs — premiums on coal production, some pass-through to coal prices, tax expenditure from deductibility, and managed-care restrictions for beneficiaries — are real but were the considered price of a self-sustaining program rather than a taxpayer bailout. The bill's chief design weakness is that its funding rests entirely on the continued vitality of the coal industry itself; benefit obligations lapse if the premium obligation ends.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 1991 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator John D. Rockefeller IV of West Virginia introduced the bill on November 19, 1991, joined by original cosponsors including Senators Byrd, Specter, Wofford, Riegle, Dixon, and Simon.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over tax and benefit legislation.
No further action was ever taken — no hearings recorded in the action history, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal producers, importers, and signatory operators were better off because the bill died: they avoided the new hourly, per-ton, and per-beneficiary premiums and the tightened obligation to keep providing retiree benefits. Retired miners and their families, meanwhile, got nothing from this bill and were left waiting on the failing plans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal companies that avoided new premiums

for.name: 14 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 13 Democrats and 1 Republican, within days of introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 19, 1991 and took no action — no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Coal industry operators
against.role: Producers, importers, and signatory companies who would owe the premiums
against.what_they_did: Opposed the industry-wide funding mechanism that would have spread legacy retiree health costs across all coal producers and importers.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 13 of 14 cosponsors were Democrats — with one Republican from coal-state Pennsylvania, but the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded party-line vote.

industries.note: Every producer would owe 75 cents per hour worked in coal production, funding retiree health care industry-wide rather than company-by-company. Ordinary retirees' coverage would be paid for out of this levy, so the industry's cost is the public benefit.
Imported coal would carry a per-ton premium (initially 15 cents) designed to equal the domestic premium, closing a loophole that would otherwise favor foreign coal over companies paying for retirees.

industries.industry: Last signatory operators (unionized coal companies and their parent companies)
industries.note: The bill locks in their obligation to keep providing benefits to existing retirees for as long as they remain in business, with parent companies jointly liable, but in exchange it caps their exposure, stops withdrawal-liability for future work, and lets managed care contain their costs.

industries.industry: United Mine Workers of America benefit funds (plan trustees and participants)
industries.note: The troubled multiemployer retiree plans are merged into a new UMWA 1991 Benefit Fund with mandatory industry assessments, making the union-benefit-plan structure the permanent channel for coal retiree health care. Retirees gain guaranteed funding; the plan system gains a stable revenue base.

industries.industry: Doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies serving coal retirees
industries.note: Mandatory managed care caps physician payments at Medicare allowable charges, imposes drug formularies and utilization review, but protects beneficiaries from balance billing and requires quality standards for provider networks.
